stories.headline: Pentagon Fires Stars and Stripes Editor, Publisher, and Reporter for Insubordination
stories.summary:
The Pentagon fired the editor-in-chief, publisher, and at least one reporter at Stars and Stripes on Friday, citing insubordination. Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin, Publisher Max Lederer, and Middle East correspondent Lara Korte all received termination notices. The firings come after the outlet — which has a long history of editorial independence despite partial taxpayer funding — clashed with Defense Department leadership over coverage, including a report on difficult conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

Stars and Stripes has operated since the Civil War era as a news outlet serving U.S. military personnel, with an institutional norm of independence from command influence. Slavin and Lederer had publicly pushed back against what they described as Pentagon interference in editorial decisions, which officials say constituted the insubordination that prompted dismissal.

Supporters of the fired staff, including press freedom advocates, argue the terminations represent a direct threat to independent military journalism and a chilling message to service members who rely on the publication for uncensored news. Pentagon officials have not offered detailed public comment on the firings beyond the insubordination designation.

The action is drawing comparisons to other Trump-era moves to reshape government media and communications. Critics on the left and among some conservatives warn that firing the editorial leadership of a historically independent military paper sets a dangerous precedent; administration allies argue leadership has the authority to enforce standards of conduct within institutions it funds.

stories.headline: Prince Harry and Co-Plaintiffs Ordered to Pay $13 Million in Failed Daily Mail Privacy Case
stories.summary:
A London High Court judge on Friday ordered Prince Harry and six co-plaintiffs — including Elton John, actor Liz Hurley, anti-racism activist Doreen Lawrence, and four others — to pay an initial 9.5 million pounds (approximately $13 million) to Associated Newspapers, publisher of the Daily Mail, following their failed invasion-of-privacy lawsuit. Justice Matthew Nicklin set a payment deadline of August 28 and described the claimants' conduct as "unreasonable to a high degree," citing the speculative nature of the claims and their failure to withdraw allegations they could no longer substantiate.

The claimants had alleged that Daily Mail journalists engaged in unlawful practices including phone hacking, but the High Court ruled against them last month. The initial payment is at the upper end of expectations; the publisher says it incurred more than 34 million pounds in costs during the case, meaning the plaintiffs could face an additional 25 million pounds in liability if Associated Newspapers pursues the remainder through costs judges.

The ruling is a significant vindication for Associated Newspapers and a major financial and reputational blow to the high-profile plaintiffs, who took out insurance covering roughly half the anticipated total costs. Legal experts said the outcome "could not have gone much worse" for the claimants, and the final amounts may be further contested before specialist costs judges.

The ruling lands as Harry and Meghan Markle are reported to be preparing to relocate from California back to the United Kingdom later this month, adding to the scrutiny surrounding the couple's return to British public life.

stories.headline: Germany Investigates Russian Links to Assassination Weapons Cache Found Near Berlin
stories.summary:
German authorities are investigating suspected Russian links to a cache of handguns and ammunition discovered in woods on the outskirts of Berlin last October, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt disclosed Friday. Federal prosecutors are examining a suspect held in Romania in connection with planned parcel bomb attacks there; Dobrindt described the individual as a "low-level agent" and said his nationality had not been disclosed. He declined to confirm the Russian connection directly but said he could not rule out "the involvement of foreign powers."

Reports in the Süddeutsche Zeitung and German public broadcasters NDR and WDR say the weapons cache was intended to facilitate targeted killings on behalf of Moscow. German security agencies have warned for months that Russian intelligence services are planning assassinations in Germany, potentially targeting defense industry executives or opposition figures living in exile.

After the weapons were rendered inoperable, authorities placed the cache under surveillance for months but observed no one approaching it. The case is the latest in a series of alleged Russian covert operations on German soil, following a 2021 court verdict sentencing a Russian national to life in prison for a Moscow-ordered murder in a Berlin park, and a 2024 CNN report alleging a Russian plot to kill Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger.

"This case demonstrates that we are operating under a high threat level," Dobrindt said. The disclosure adds pressure on European governments to harden counterintelligence postures as the war in Ukraine continues.

stories.headline: First U.S. Deportation Flight to Haiti Departs Since TPS Ended for 350,000 Haitians
stories.summary:
The Trump administration carried out its first deportation flight to Haiti since Temporary Protected Status (TPS) expired for more than 350,000 Haitian nationals in June, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed Friday. An ICE flight carrying 161 passengers departed from Alexandria, Louisiana, and landed at Cap Haitien Airport on Thursday. It is not yet confirmed whether former TPS holders were among those on board.

The Supreme Court cleared the way for the administration to end TPS for Haiti and several other countries — including Ethiopia, Somalia, Syria, and Myanmar — in a June order. The administration had previously conducted deportation flights to Haiti, but Thursday's flight is the first since the TPS protections lapsed, marking a new phase of enforcement against a population that had been shielded from removal for years.

Haitian immigrants and immigrant-rights advocates have expressed alarm, warning that many deportees face dangerous conditions in Haiti amid ongoing gang violence and political instability. The administration has separately been monitoring hundreds of former TPS holders in Ohio, some of whom have been fitted with ankle monitors following in-person check-ins with DHS.

The flight came on the same day a third-country deportation flight landed in Liberia, marking the first forced transfer to that country under a recently signed deportation agreement with Washington. Together, the actions reflect the administration's accelerating push to expand and execute its deportation agenda across multiple regions simultaneously.

stories.headline: Russian Double-Tap Drone Strike on Ukrainian Mall Kills 15, Injures 130
stories.summary:
A Russian drone attack on a crowded shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih, the central Ukrainian city that is also President Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown, killed at least 15 people and injured 130 others, including 23 children, Ukrainian officials said Friday. The strike was carried out in two waves, with a second drone hitting the already-burning mall as emergency workers responded to the first explosion — a tactic known as a double-tap attack. Rescue teams from four other Ukrainian regions were deployed to search for survivors still trapped in the rubble.

Zelensky condemned the attack as "absolutely cynical and despicable," saying it deliberately targeted first responders. Dramatic footage verified by BBC News shows the second drone striking the burning structure. Russia's military had not commented on the attack as of Friday evening.

The Kryvyi Rih strike was part of a broader day of Russian attacks. Four people, including three children, were killed in Ukraine's southern Mykolaiv region, and two more were killed in the northeast Kharkiv region. The assault follows a major Russian missile and drone barrage on Kyiv the previous day that killed 17 people and damaged residential buildings, a children's hospital, and a school.

Earlier Friday, Ukraine's military said it struck an oil refinery and a military airfield deep inside Russia. Kyiv has intensified attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in recent months, describing such targets as legitimate because they help finance Moscow's war effort. Russia currently controls roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory in the country's southeast.

stories.headline: DOJ and TikTok Settle Children's Privacy Lawsuit for $400 Million
stories.summary:
The U.S. Justice Department and TikTok, along with its Chinese parent company ByteDance, have agreed to a $400 million settlement resolving allegations that the app violated the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), according to an announcement first shared with Axios. The Biden administration's DOJ originally filed the suit in 2024. TikTok will pay the sum without admitting wrongdoing and without undergoing further litigation.

The $400 million payment is described as being at the upper end of expectations for a settlement of this kind and represents one of the largest penalties ever assessed under children's online privacy law. COPPA prohibits companies from collecting personal data on children under 13 without verifiable parental consent.

The settlement resolves a major outstanding legal liability for TikTok at a moment when the platform has been navigating intense scrutiny in Washington over its data practices and its ties to ByteDance. The company has faced repeated congressional hearings and legislation targeting its U.S. operations.

The agreement does not require TikTok to alter its data collection practices beyond what may be specified in a consent decree, details of which were expected to be released alongside the formal settlement filing. Child safety advocates have called for stronger structural remedies beyond financial penalties.

stories.headline: SNAP Enrollment Falls More Than 13% as 'Big Beautiful Bill' Work Requirements Take Hold
stories.summary:
Enrollment in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program dropped by more than 13 percent over a 12-month period, a decline far steeper than federal government projections, as work requirements and other provisions of President Trump's budget and tax legislation — dubbed the "big beautiful bill" — began taking effect. The data represent the most concrete evidence yet of the law's impact on the country's largest federally funded food assistance program.

Supporters of the changes, including the Trump administration and Republican lawmakers who passed the legislation, argue that work requirements are a necessary reform to ensure that able-bodied adults are engaged in employment or job training, reducing dependency on federal assistance and generating long-term savings. They contend the steeper-than-expected drop reflects successful enforcement of existing eligibility rules.

Critics, including anti-hunger advocates and congressional Democrats, warn the sharp enrollment decline signals that eligible recipients — including families with children, elderly individuals, and people with disabilities — are being incorrectly removed from the rolls due to administrative burdens associated with the new requirements. They argue the drop exceeds any plausible reduction in actual need.

The SNAP program serves tens of millions of low-income Americans and is one of the largest domestic safety net programs in the federal budget. The extent of the enrollment decline is expected to intensify the political debate over the bill's social consequences heading into the midterm election cycle.

stories.headline: Texas Court Slashes $50 Million Sandy Hook Judgment Against Alex Jones to About $6 Million
stories.summary:
A Texas appeals court on Friday reduced a $50 million jury judgment against Infowars founder Alex Jones to approximately $6 million, ruling that the trial judge had improperly allowed plaintiffs to seek punitive damages beyond the state's statutory cap. The court left intact $4.1 million in compensatory damages awarded to Sandy Hook parents Neil Heslin and Scarlett Lewis, whose six-year-old son Jesse was among the 26 people killed in the 2012 Newtown, Connecticut massacre, but cut punitive damages from more than $45 million down to $1.5 million to comply with Texas's $750,000-per-plaintiff cap.

The Texas Third Court of Appeals found unanimously that Heslin and Lewis did not present sufficient evidence that the harassment they suffered as a result of Jones's false hoax claims reached the threshold required to exceed the statutory cap. The panel also found the trial judge erred in permitting the parents to pursue higher damages after the trial concluded.

Jones, who spent years falsely claiming the Sandy Hook shooting was staged by the government to justify gun control, called the ruling "a gigantic victory for the First Amendment" on his streaming show Friday and vowed to continue appealing the case to the Texas Supreme Court. Attorneys for Heslin and Lewis dismissed the ruling as "irrelevant," noting that Jones still faces a separate $1.25 billion judgment in Connecticut and has yet to make any payments on any of the financial judgments against him.

The ruling does not affect the Connecticut judgment and comes as Jones continues to contest efforts to liquidate his company, Free Speech Systems. The case drew national attention and is widely seen as a landmark in holding media figures financially liable for defamation that incites harassment of private citizens.

stories.headline: At Least 48 Dead After Overloaded Boat Capsizes in Northwestern Nigeria
stories.summary:
At least 48 people were killed Thursday when an overloaded wooden boat carrying an estimated 70 passengers capsized on a river in the remote Gorau area of Sokoto state in northwestern Nigeria. Victims were mostly farmers and children heading to rice fields along the riverbanks when the vessel, which had developed a leak, took on water and sank. Around 10 people are reported rescued, with search and rescue operations continuing overnight.

Local lawmaker Bashir Usman Gorau confirmed to the BBC that many of the victims were children, who commonly accompany parents to farms during harvest season. The remote location, poor road access, and unreliable mobile phone coverage have hampered relief efforts. Nigeria's emergency management agency dispatched a team to the area, though security services were initially unable to reach the scene due to the presence of armed criminal gangs operating in the region.

Boat accidents are endemic in Nigeria, routinely attributed to overcrowding, poorly maintained vessels, and weak enforcement of maritime safety regulations. In December 2024, 54 bodies were recovered from the River Niger after a boat possibly carrying more than 200 passengers capsized. Authorities have repeatedly recommended measures including the provision of life jackets, deployment of water guards at jetties, and mandatory training for boat operators, but implementation has remained inconsistent.

The Sokoto region is additionally challenged by the presence of militant and jihadist groups, including Lakurawa, which has been active in the state and neighboring Kebbi state. The insecurity has forced many communities to abandon their homes and complicates emergency response in rural areas.

stories.headline: Sword Attack at Swedish High School Leaves Two Teenagers Seriously Injured
stories.summary:
Two teenagers were seriously injured Friday afternoon in a sword attack at Brinell School in Fagersta, Sweden, police confirmed. Officers arrested one man at the scene, and local media reported the suspect was shot in the leg by police during the response. A third person was also wounded, with the extent of their injuries not yet confirmed. Eight surrounding schools were placed under lockdown, which has since been lifted, and a state of high alert was declared across the Vastmanland region.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson described the incident as a 'serious attack' on X, noting that authorities were working intensively to understand the circumstances. The attack came within days of students returning from summer break, with the new term having begun on Monday or Wednesday depending on the academic year. Brinell School has just under 500 students and is located roughly 170 kilometers northwest of Stockholm.

The attack is the latest in a series of violent incidents at Swedish educational institutions in recent years. Sweden's worst-ever mass shooting occurred in 2025 when 11 people, including the gunman, died at an adult education center in Orebro, prompting the government to tighten gun laws. Two teachers were killed at a Malmo secondary school in 2022, and a teacher and pupil were killed in a sword attack in Trollhattan in 2015.

Sweden has faced intensifying public debate over crime and security, particularly around attacks on schools and public spaces. Friday's attack is expected to renew scrutiny of security measures in educational settings and the broader challenge of violent crime in the country.

stories.headline: Five Missing After Fire Destroys Restaurant and Apartments in Swiss Alpine Town
stories.summary:
Five people are missing and eight others were injured after a fire completely destroyed a restaurant with apartments above it in the Swiss town of Thusis in the early hours of Friday morning. Graubünden cantonal police said the blaze broke out on the second floor shortly after midnight local time, with nearly 100 firefighters responding. The stairwell collapsed during the fire, requiring a crane to open the roof and allow access to search for survivors.

Fourteen people managed to escape the building; two suffered serious injuries, two moderate injuries, and four minor injuries. Those injured were transported to hospitals in the neighboring towns of Chur, Thusis, Ilanz, and Zurich. Police noted that a number of foreign nationals were among those staying in the building at the time, consistent with Thusis's status as a tourist destination in the popular Graubünden alpine region.

Emergency personnel are removing the roof layer by layer to access the collapsed stairwell in the ongoing search for the five missing individuals. Police and the public prosecutor's office have launched an investigation into the cause of the fire. A cantonal police spokeswoman indicated the search could last for days, and DNA samples will be taken if human remains are found.

The cause of the fire remains unknown as of Friday. Thusis is located in the Graubünden canton of eastern Switzerland, a region known for winter sports and summer alpine tourism that draws visitors from across Europe.

stories.headline: Former Abercrombie & Fitch CEO Mike Jeffries Ruled Competent to Stand Trial on Sex Trafficking Charges
stories.summary:
A federal judge ruled Friday that former Abercrombie & Fitch CEO Mike Jeffries is mentally competent to stand trial on sex trafficking and prostitution charges, reversing an earlier finding. Judge Nusrat Choudhury issued the ruling after reviewing Jeffries' medical records and more than 21 hours of audio recordings from 109 phone calls. The judge found 'ample evidence' that Jeffries possesses a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings against him. His trial is scheduled to begin October 26.

Jeffries, 81, had been declared mentally incompetent by a court last year on the basis that he was suffering from dementia and late-onset Alzheimer's disease. Judge Choudhury said the phone recordings were 'particularly illuminating,' finding Jeffries to be 'a fluent conversational partner' capable of learning new information. The court will nonetheless make accommodations for his age and cognitive impairments, including limiting court hours to 1:00–5:00 p.m. and allowing multiple breaks during proceedings.

Jeffries, his partner Matthew Smith, and alleged middleman James Jacobson were charged in October 2024 with operating a global sex trafficking and prostitution enterprise. All three have pleaded not guilty; a conviction could carry a maximum sentence of life in prison. The charges followed a 2023 BBC investigation and podcast series that revealed the trio allegedly ran a sophisticated operation scouting young men for sex around the world during Jeffries' tenure as CEO.

The case drew significant public attention upon the initial BBC investigation and the subsequent arrests. The ruling clears the final legal obstacle before trial and is expected to renew scrutiny of how corporate power and wealth were allegedly used to facilitate abuse. More than 40 men have come forward with accusations against Jeffries.

stories.headline: Update: Russian Airstrikes Kill at Least 17 Civilians Across Ukraine; Zelensky Pleads for Patriot Missiles
stories.summary:
Russia launched a massive overnight assault on Ukraine involving several ballistic and cruise missiles and an estimated 168 drones, killing at least 17 civilians and injuring more than 40 others. The attack, one of the largest in recent weeks, targeted multiple cities. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called on Western allies to urgently replenish Ukraine's Patriot interceptor stockpiles, warning that supplies have dwindled to dangerously low levels.

A retired U.S. Army colonel present in Kyiv during the strike described the attack as consistent with Russia's practice of marshaling missiles for periodic large-scale barrages, typically once or twice a week. Ukrainian air defenses, aided by intelligence sharing with the United States, provided hours of advance warning via Telegram channels, allowing civilians to reach shelters. Analysts say Russia is using deliberate targeting of civilian infrastructure as a strategic tool.

Zelensky stressed that Ukraine is prepared to purchase the weapons outright rather than receive them as aid, but that only partner nations can supply what is needed. The depletion of air defense assets has raised alarm among Ukrainian officials and Western military observers about Ukraine's ability to protect critical infrastructure from future strikes.

The assault underscores the continuing intensity of the conflict more than four years after Russia's full-scale invasion. Ukraine has simultaneously been conducting long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, contributing to significant fuel shortages inside Russia — a development that military analysts say is beginning to erode Russian logistics and civilian morale.

stories.headline: Ukrainian Drone Strikes Trigger Severe Fuel Shortages Across Moscow as Russia Imports Petrol
stories.summary:
Sustained Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have triggered a second wave of fuel shortages across Moscow and other parts of Russia, with motorists queuing for hours at petrol stations — in some cases overnight — only to find pumps run dry. Russian officials attribute the disruptions to "unscheduled repairs" at oil refineries damaged by the attacks. The crisis has grown worse than an earlier shortage this summer, with observers noting the government is struggling to resolve both refining capacity and logistics problems.

In an extraordinary move for one of the world's leading crude oil exporters, Russia has begun importing petrol to ease the domestic shortage. The government has also temporarily authorized the production and sale of lower-grade Euro 2 petrol — banned in Russia since 2013 — which contains up to 50 times more sulfur than modern standards and can damage modern vehicle engines with extended use.

The shortages are emerging alongside visible patriotic messaging on billboards across Moscow marking Russian Flag Day, highlighting a stark contrast between state-projected confidence and civilian hardship. Russian broadsheets are describing the situation as a "second wave of the fuel crisis," and the government has acknowledged the need for additional measures.

The development represents a tangible domestic consequence of the war for ordinary Russians and signals that Ukraine's long-range strike campaign on energy infrastructure is achieving measurable strategic effect. The Kremlin has shown no indication of altering its military course in response.

stories.headline: Update: Oil Markets Growing Immune to Trump's Social Media Posts on Iran War
stories.summary:
An Axios analysis finds that oil price movements in response to President Trump's Truth Social posts about the Iran war have been shrinking significantly over time, even as the conflict continues to cause major supply disruptions in global energy markets. Traders initially moved markets sharply on Trump's posts, which carried signals about potential U.S. military actions or diplomatic shifts affecting oil transit through the Strait of Hormuz. That sensitivity has diminished as the war has extended beyond six months with no clear resolution.

The trend matters because oil price swings ripple through the broader U.S. and global economies, affecting consumer prices at the pump, inflation, and borrowing costs. Analysts suggest traders have grown more skeptical that individual presidential statements reliably predict policy outcomes, particularly as Trump's own officials have made claims about Hormuz oil traffic that market analysts have questioned.

Trump this week described his strategy against Iran as "economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale," telling reporters he is counting on sanctions after what he characterized as abandoning a bombing campaign. The administration has framed Iran as severely weakened; critics and some analysts argue that the regime's survival through months of conflict has demonstrated resilience that contradicts early U.S. assessments.

The story is covered by twelve outlets across the political spectrum, reflecting its significance for both energy markets and the broader conduct of the Iran war. It also intersects with ongoing concerns in Washington about Treasury bond yields hitting near-20-year highs, as energy costs and war-related uncertainty continue to weigh on the fiscal outlook.

stories.headline: Update: Data Centers Become Midterm Electoral Liability as Candidates in Both Parties Scramble for Position
stories.summary:
A growing anti-data center backlash is reshaping midterm election dynamics across the country, with candidates from both parties distancing themselves from the AI infrastructure projects their own leaders spent years courting. In Michigan, Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers called this week for a one-year moratorium on new data center construction — a sign of how politically toxic the issue has become even among candidates who previously supported technology investment. New York Governor Kathy Hochul (D) is positioning herself as a Democratic alternative, advocating a "thoughtful" regulatory approach rather than outright opposition.

What began as scattered local opposition rooted in concerns about noise, energy consumption, water use and land use has scaled into a national cross-partisan movement. Campaigns in key Senate battlegrounds, including Michigan and Ohio, are now treating data centers as a defining issue. The GOP Senate campaign arm has privately warned that data centers are becoming an electoral liability, according to prior reporting.

Supporters of data center expansion argue the facilities are essential to maintaining U.S. competitiveness in artificial intelligence and that restricting construction would cede ground to China. Opponents — including environmental groups, local residents and some labor advocates — contend the projects strain local power grids, consume vast quantities of water and deliver fewer local jobs than promised.

The political shift represents a significant rupture in the bipartisan consensus that enabled rapid AI infrastructure buildout over the past several years. How candidates navigate the issue in competitive races this fall could influence both technology policy and the balance of power in Congress.

stories.headline: Eight killed in plane crash at remote Alaskan military radar site
stories.summary:
A civilian-contracted aircraft carrying eight people crashed near Cape Newenham, Alaska, on Thursday shortly after noon local time, killing everyone on board. The plane had departed Anchorage International Airport bound for a remote US Air Force long-range radar site roughly 450 miles to the west. Search and rescue teams reached the crash site and confirmed there were no survivors among the two pilots and six passengers.

Cape Newenham is part of the Alaska Radar System, a network of remote installations that monitor aircraft approaching or operating in Alaskan airspace. Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, chief of the US Air Force Alaskan Command, described those killed as 'dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment' and said the Air Force's priority is supporting the families of the deceased. An investigation is under way, and identities will be released once next of kin are notified.

The National Transportation Safety Board's Alaska regional chief, Clint Johnson, confirmed the breakdown of two pilots and six passengers aboard the aircraft. The cause of the crash has not been determined. The remote and rugged terrain of southwestern Alaska presents significant logistical challenges for investigation and recovery operations.

stories.headline: Hong Kong activists convicted under national security law for organizing Tiananmen vigils
stories.summary:
A Hong Kong court on Friday found veteran pro-democracy activists Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung guilty of inciting others to subvert state power under the city's Beijing-imposed national security law. The two had been leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which organized annual candlelight vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown — events that made Hong Kong one of the only places in Chinese territory where such public memorials were held. A third defendant, Albert Ho, pleaded guilty in January. All three face a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison, with sentencing set for a later date.

Authorities banned the vigils in 2020, initially citing Covid-19 restrictions, but they have never been permitted to resume. The national security law, which took effect that same year, criminalizes a broad range of dissenting acts. Chinese authorities have long sought to suppress any public acknowledgment of the Tiananmen crackdown on the mainland, where even oblique references are censored.

Human rights organizations condemned the verdicts. Amnesty International said the case 'relies on vague, overly broad and arbitrary definitions of subversion' and called Lee and Chow 'prisoners of conscience who should never have been prosecuted.' Human Rights Watch said the convictions demonstrated that 'public displays of mourning have become a crime in Hong Kong.' The verdict is seen as a further marker of Hong Kong's transformation from a city with robust civil liberties under 'one country, two systems' to one governed by mainland-style political restrictions.

stories.headline: Update: Israel re-establishes West Bank settlement shuttered for 20 years, defying international criticism
stories.summary:
Thirty Israeli settler families returned Thursday to Kadim, a settlement in the northern West Bank near Jenin that had been dismantled in 2005 under then-Prime Minister Ariel Sharon's unilateral Disengagement Plan. The re-establishment of Kadim, overseen with government backing and some military escort, marks the first time settlers have returned to any of the four northern West Bank settlements evacuated as part of that plan. All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal under international law.

Israel's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich presided over the opening ceremony alongside the Justice Minister and the Speaker of the Knesset. Smotrich framed the return as a 'correction' of what he called the 'crime of expulsion,' using the Biblical term for the northern West Bank. The head of the regional settlers' council vowed that settlers would one day return to Gaza as well.

Palestinian residents of surrounding villages expressed fear over the renewed settlement activity, with one farmer describing how settlers had already driven his nephews from their agricultural land. The move comes amid sustained international pressure over Israeli settlement expansion: the UK, France, Germany, Italy, and Canada have previously condemned a related West Bank settlement tender. Critics argue the re-establishment of Kadim deepens the fragmentation of Palestinian territory and forecloses the possibility of a contiguous Palestinian state.

stories.headline: Panama Canal to cut daily ship transits by 11% starting September amid El Niño drought
stories.summary:
The Panama Canal Authority announced Thursday it will reduce the number of vessels permitted to transit the waterway daily from 36 to 32 beginning September 15, citing low water levels caused by a stronger-than-usual El Niño weather pattern. The phased reductions will begin September 3. Canal officials said the cuts are necessary to preserve long-term service reliability and to protect freshwater supplies for human consumption in the surrounding region.

The restriction compounds already significant stress on global shipping. The Iran war has sharply reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's other critical maritime chokepoints, forcing carriers to reroute through longer and more expensive passages. The Panama Canal handles roughly 14,000 vessel transits per year and generates approximately $3 billion annually for Panama — making any reduction consequential both for the country's finances and for global supply chains.

Forecasters expect this year's El Niño to rank among the strongest on record, with effects amplified by long-term climate change. The canal faced a similar but less severe restriction in 2023 during the last El Niño cycle, when Panama recorded its driest October since 1950. Since then the authority has implemented water-saving measures, but officials said additional steps were still required to ensure the canal's sustained operation.
